Issued at 245 AM CDT Fri Oct 9 2026

The main concern over the next couple of days will be warm 
temperatures and strong winds contributing to fire weather concerns 
for the next couple of days. Starting with the winds today, a 
tightening pressure gradient stemming from a low pressure center to 
the northwest will increase southerly winds today, particularly 
along the Missouri River. In that area, gusts may reach up to 30-35 
miles per hour, while elsewhere gusts up to 25-30 miles per hour 
will be present. Highs will be in the upper 70s to low 80s over much 
of the area, but up into the mid 80s over parts of central South 
Dakota. These temperatures are about 15-20 degrees above normal for 
this time of year. Generally not expecting any records to be set 
today despite the abnormal warmth, although Pierre and Aberdeen are 
both within 5 degrees of their daily record highs. 

Saturday will see further warm air advection into the region, 
partially coming in the form of a 40-50 knot low-level jet. The warm 
air advection will push 850mb temperatures as high as 25-26 Celsius 
over much of the area, which is both about 10 degree increase from 
Friday and 10 degrees above the 90th percentile for this time of 
year. Naturally, this will provide a further warmup to the area, and 
temperatures closer to the NBM 90th percentile can be expected under 
the clear sky, warm air advection regime. This will push highs into 
the upper 80s to low 90s across much of the forecast area. Even with 
this significantly abnormal heat, record highs are still a few 
degrees above the current forecast at most sites, with the exception 
of Watertown forecast to break their record of 86 degrees. The 
aforementioned low-level jet will be mainly over eastern South 
Dakota and western Minnesota by Saturday afternoon when gusts will 
be able to mix to the surface. Generally expecting  25-35 miles per 
hour once again, although this time the area of focus for these 
higher winds will be from Brown and Spink Counties and east. 
However, wind will be coming from a favorable direction to induce 
downslope winds off the Prairie Coteau, and gusts as high as 45 
miles per hour may be possible on the eastern side of the Coteau. At 
this point can't rule out the potential for a limited-area Wind 
Advisory Saturday afternoon, although nothing will be issued with 
this forecast package. The wind and heat combination will cause 
elevated fire weather concerns over much of the area. Over the 
northeast with the strongest winds, minimum humidity in the 
afternoon will drop between 25-35 percent, so right on the 
borderline of the 25 percent criteria for a Red Flag Warning. Parts 
of central South Dakota may also need a Red Flag Warning, as 
humidity will drop below 20 percent west of the Missouri River, 
which combines with gusts of 25 miles per hour. All this to say, 
watch out for potential headlines with future forecast packages. 

The next chances for rain will come on Monday. A small shortwave 
disturbance accompanied by some divergence aloft will produce these 
showers, but the lack of any strong forcing mechanism will keep rain 
rates fairly low. Expect the majority of the rain to fall over north 
central South Dakota, perhaps extending into northeastern South 
Dakota along the border with North Dakota. Latest NBM probabilities 
to see a tenth of an inch through Monday night range from 10-40% 
across the forecast area, increasing as you move from southeast to 
northwest. Model soundings over far north central South Dakota do 
show some borderline potential for a profile cold enough to carry 
frozen hydrometeors into the lower levels or perhaps the surface, 
but this would most likely be an edge case. Even if some flurries 
are able to fall, chances for sub-freezing surface temperatures are 
less than 10 percent, so should this edge case come to be, these 
flurries would almost certainly melt upon contact with the surface. 

Looking ahead to mid-week, ensemble clusters show a decent level of 
agreement (~62% of total members) in a pattern that would develop a 
Colorado Low up into the Northern Plains. This will bring the next 
chances for precipitation into the region, although there is still a 
high degree of spread in totals at this point. Heaviest rainfall is 
currently expected overnight Wednesday into Thursday, and near-
surface low temperatures during that period will remain in the 40s 
so all rain can be expected. The same can't be said with as much 
certainty on the tail end of the event, as parts of the Aberdeen 
forecast area have a 10-30% chance for overnight lows Thursday night 
into Friday morning to reach below freezing.
